model.comments: High effort Claude Fable 5.1. Thinking is always on for Fable; depth is controlled by Anthropic's output_config.effort, which OpenRouter sets from reasoning.effort (its verbosity field maps to the same native field, so this equals the older opus-4.x verbosity convention).

prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Clobber game on a 5x6 grid. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(you: list[int], opponent: list[int]) -> str: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - Board size is 5 rows x 6 columns. - `you` and `opponent` are 5x6 arrays describing the board. - Values are 0 or 1. - `you[row, col] == 1` means you have a piece at cell `(row, col)`. - `opponent[row, col] == 1` means the opponent has a piece at cell `(row, col)`. - For any `(row, col)`, at most one of `you[row, col]` and `opponent[row, col]` is 1. # Action / Return Format - Return a string move in the format `'row,col,dir'`. - `row` is the row of the starting cell (0-4). - `col` is the column of the starting cell (0-5). - `dir` is the direction of the move: `'U'` (up), `'R'` (right), `'D'` (down), `'L'` (left). - The start cell must contain your piece. - The destination cell must be in bounds and contain an opponent piece. - A legal move must capture an adjacent opponent piece by moving one square orthogonally onto it. - The opponent piece is removed; your piece occupies the destination square; your starting square becomes empty. - The first player to have no legal moves on their turn loses. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm designing a Clobber policy for a 5x6 board, considering alpha-beta search with iterative deepening under a time budget, combined with a mobility-based evaluation function. Given 30 cells and roughly 15 pieces per side initially, full game-tree solving isn't realistic in Python within a second, so I'm aiming for moderate search depth backed by solid heuristics.

Legal moves come from checking adjacent cells for opposing pieces to capture, and the search uses negamax with alpha-beta pruning, a transposition table, and time checks to enable iterative deepening. My evaluation centers on mobility difference, and since Clobber positions can fragment into independent components as pieces get captured, exact search becomes feasible once the piece count drops low enough. I'll also make sure the agent always returns a legal move by wrapping the logic in a try/except with a fallback, and I'm representing the board using bitboards as Python integers with shift operations for adjacency, indexing cells as row*6+col for efficient move generation.

For evaluation, I'll use mobility difference (my moves minus opponent moves) scaled up, since more available moves tends to favor the player in Clobber endgames. I'm budgeting around 0.7 seconds for the search with periodic time checks, and skipping component decomposition for simplicity despite it being a possible optimization. Now I'm setting up the board constants and column masks for move generation.

Writing move generation logic...

I'll represent moves as source/destination bit pairs, applying them by updating the piece bitboards and switching to the opponent's turn via negamax recursion. For the search, I'm using a transposition table for move ordering, checking node counts and terminal conditions where no moves means a loss, and adjusting win scores based on depth to prefer faster wins.

My evaluation function will compare mobility between the two players, and I'm considering a cheap one-ply lookahead heuristic to order moves by predicted opponent mobility after each candidate move, since good ordering matters a lot for alpha-beta pruning efficiency. I'm planning iterative deepening up to depth 40, stopping early on time limits or forced wins, and keeping the best move from the last fully completed depth.

Setting up constants and helper functions...

Now I need to convert bit indices to move notation: computing row/col from the bit index, and determining direction from src-to-dst offset. I'll assume row 0 is at the top, so up decreases the row index by 6 — the standard convention, though there's some risk if the arena defines it oppositely.

Now I'm implementing negamax search with alpha-beta pruning and a transposition table: generating legal moves, returning a mobility-based heuristic at leaf depth, checking the timeout deadline periodically, and probing the TT for cached bounds and a move hint to try first.

I finish storing the transposition table entry with the flag and best move, then think about a potential optimization: since the move ordering already computes child mobility, at depth 1 I could shortcut and reuse that value directly instead of recursing again.

That shortcut works because the mobility difference at depth 1 essentially equals the negated score unless the opponent has no moves, in which case it's a win. Then I move on to setting up the root-level iterative deepening search with a policy function that converts the board into bitboards.

For the root loop, if there are no legal moves I just return a default no-op action. Otherwise I run manual iterative deepening with a time budget of about 0.75 seconds, capping search depth by the number of pieces remaining on the board since each move removes exactly one piece, and I also add an early exit if the best score already reaches a winning value.

I keep a transposition table across calls but clear it if it grows past a couple million entries, and I decide the mobility-difference evaluation is sufficient given the search depth, so I'll skip more elaborate heuristics. I need to make sure any timeout exception raised deep in the search during root iterative deepening gets caught so I can break cleanly and fall back on the best move found so far.

Given the throughput I expect in Python, roughly 100k-200k nodes per second, depth 5-6 midgame search seems achievable, so I'm ready to finalize the code.
